question: What were the cities of the Indus Valley generally enclosed with?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Fortified walls with gateways**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The cities of the **Indus Valley Civilization** were generally enclosed with **fortified walls** that included gateways, indicating a focus on urban planning and security.
 
• The fortified walls served multiple purposes such as **defense against potential invasions**, protection against floods, and demarcation of the city’s boundaries.
 
• These walls were constructed using baked bricks of uniform size, showcasing the **advanced engineering skills** and **standardization** techniques of the Indus Valley people.
 
• Prominent cities like **Harappa**, **Mohenjo-Daro**, and **Kalibangan** were known for having these fortified structures, which often separated the **citadel** (upper town) from the lower residential area.
 
• The gateways in the walls were used not only for entry and exit but also for **trade, taxation, and monitoring movement**. This highlights the economic and administrative sophistication of the civilization.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Indus Valley Civilization:**

 
 
• The Indus Valley Civilization (2600-1900 BCE) is one of the world’s oldest urban civilizations, thriving in areas of present-day **India and Pakistan**.
 
• It is renowned for its **meticulous urban planning**, with well-laid streets, drainage systems, and large public baths.
 
• Key cities include **Harappa** (Punjab, Pakistan), **Mohenjo-Daro** (Sindh, Pakistan), and **Dholavira** (Gujarat, India).
 
 
 
• **Construction Techniques:**
 
 
• The walls were primarily made of **baked bricks**, a notable feature distinguishing the Indus Valley Civilization from other contemporary civilizations.
 
• The use of standardized brick sizes suggests a centralized authority overseeing construction practices.
 
 
 
• **Purpose of Fortified Walls:**
 
 
• **Defense:** The walls protected the inhabitants from invaders and natural calamities like floods.
 
• **Urban Organization:** The walls demarcated administrative areas (citadel) from residential ones, reflecting a hierarchical society.
 
• **Trade Control:** The gateways in the walls allowed for regulation of trade and collection of taxes.
 
 
 
• **Other Features of Indus Valley Cities:**
 
 
• Advanced drainage systems with covered drains and soak pits indicate a focus on hygiene and sanitation.
 
• Public buildings, granaries, and baths like the **Great Bath of Mohenjo-Daro** highlight the civilization’s architectural achievements.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Option 1: Wooden fences**

 
 
• Wooden fences were not a feature of Indus Valley cities. Wood was primarily used for making tools, carts, and furniture rather than for constructing large structures.
 
 
 
• **Option 3: Stone barricades**
 
 
• Stone was rarely used in Indus construction. Baked bricks were the dominant material, reflecting the availability of resources like clay in the region.
 
 
 
• **Option 4: Moats and drawbridges**
 
 
• While moats and drawbridges were common in medieval forts, there is no archaeological evidence of such structures in Indus Valley cities.
 
 
 
• Indus Valley’s focus on fortified walls with gateways was a unique feature of its urban planning, serving both practical and administrative purposes.
